We have Grafana monitoring everything from the usual cloud stuff down to the temperatures of cryogenic fridges. Being able to configure alerts more dynamically and clearly in Grafana 8 will make my job a lot easier.

I find the new panels in Grafana 8 really useful, but I'm not sure I like the color changes to the navbar and panel backgrounds. The new colors feel a little washed out compared to the darker grays in v7.x.

The Node graph visualization couldn't be used with just any datasource, even with data shaped as node and edge frames, because it needed a special meta property. Also wish an embedded panel could select its own time range.
Over the years I've evaluated multiple other solutions like Grafana, but none of them came even near Grafana's feature set and simplicity.

Before Grafana, Graphite's render endpoint was decent but Grafana was the first tool that let you easily make nice-looking graphs and dashboards. Looking forward to Library panels, a feature I always found lacking.
I use Graphite, InfluxDB, PostgreSQL, Timescale, CloudWatch and Prometheus. Grafana alerting supporting all those variations is a godsend.

Use case: alerting on billing throughput in a third-party billing system with an RDBMS backend that isn't instrumented with Prometheus. The alert can be written in SQL and, with Grafana 8, routed just like Prometheus alerts.

Grafana is the de facto realtime graph consolidation platform where I work. If a monitoring tool doesn't interact with Grafana, don't bother deploying it, because the rest of the org will be blind to it.

In our biophysics lab I set up Grafana and InfluxDB to show equipment output during experiments as a gimmick. It became our preferred way to watch experiments, far more useful than the manufacturer's software, though some cases felt outside Grafana's intended use.
I love using Grafana, but I abhor creating dashboards and trying to pull data, mostly because of a lack of documentation.
The AGPL license change prevents me from using Grafana at work. Here's to being stuck on 7.x!
Grafana 8 is the first release under AGPL. A major licensing change like that should have been called out in the changelog.

Grafana used to be so simple; not a fan of the direction toward many services. Running and configuring Alertmanager alongside Grafana was bad enough, and now OnCall is another service. Upgrading from Grafana 7 also left 'legacy alerts'.

Cost is the big selling point of Grafana Cloud: far cheaper than most competitors and good enough. It's not as good as New Relic or Datadog, but you get decent metrics, logs, alerts, tracing and incident management at an excellent price.

Even though we use Grafana only internally and AGPLv3 should be no problem in theory, I see big meetings with legal coming that might stop us from using it. Other corporations likely face the same, which could hurt Grafana's popularity.

I wonder how many companies will drop Grafana over the AGPL change. Two companies I've worked for simply banned anything with a GPL-type license. In commercial settings, GPL is poison and AGPL is radioactive poison.
I wish people would stop equating Grafana's move with Elastic's. Grafana switched from one FOSS license to another; Elastic switched from a FOSS license to a proprietary one.

Grafana moves really fast and is very practical, from InfluxDB/ES config storage to SQLite to MySQL/Postgres, then alerting and multiple data sources. My team even uses it with SQL as a cheap version of Periscope/Mode.
I signed up, sent logs from a k8s cluster and set up the Loki data source on the hosted instance, but couldn't find a way to actually explore the logs in the hosted Grafana instance.
Loki looks like a good lightweight alternative to setting up a full Elasticsearch cluster for light log insights, though the free cloud demo was getting hammered at launch.

Even though we only use Grafana internally and AGPLv3 should be fine in theory, the user expects big meetings with legal that could end with them no longer being allowed to use it, and suspects other corporations will be in the same position.
Two companies this user worked for banned anything with a GPL-type license, so they wonder how many companies will drop Grafana after the AGPLv3 relicense.

Users who ship Grafana in a Docker container with their product, or embed Grafana dashboards in a SaaS, are unsure whether AGPL forces their own code open. One says the announcement and the AGPL text seem to conflict about larger works that include Grafana.

Complaint: AGPL makes it impossible to reuse Grafana/Loki/Tempo pieces or libraries in permissively licensed code without forcing that whole project into AGPL, which hurts interoperability. Only some parts were exempted.
"Over the years I've evaluated multiple other solutions like Grafana but none of them came even near the feature set and simplicity of Grafana."

Grafana is the de facto realtime graph consolidation platform at this user's workplace: if a monitoring tool doesn't integrate with Grafana, deploying it isn't worth it because the rest of the org will be blind to it.

Likes the new Grafana 8 panels but isn't sure about the color changes to the navbar and panel backgrounds. Another user says the uPlot change is amazing and the canvas-based rendering seems very fast.
"I love using grafana however I abhor creating dashboards and trying to pull data, but that's mostly because of a lack of documentation."

Regrets upgrading to Grafana 8 with InfluxDB 2. Category names now include '_value' with no fix short of hundreds of overrides. Two-axis line charts merged into one axis, making a series unreadable. Legend columns can't be easily reordered or sorted. Legend rows no longer work with Vimium.
The same user praises the 'Connect null values' feature as a lifesaver: gaps from unreliable third-party sensors now show as proper empty gaps instead of misleading interpolated data.

Used Grafana with collectd and InfluxDB for personal servers, but after updates couldn't replicate their queries and went back to plain RRDTool with static HTML. Still thinks Grafana is a great product but feels it has drifted into 'enterprise' territory, too complicated for personal use.

"I love Grafana" but feels the company now releases too much too soon. This morning all their dashboards stopped working after their Grafana Cloud account was upgraded to v9, with no stable release or breaking-change documentation. Grafana rolled the account back.

Wishes it were easier to mix Grafana SaaS and self-hosted products. They must self-host Loki for privacy but would use hosted Tempo/Prometheus/OnCall, and linking self-hosted Loki queries with SaaS Prometheus isn't easy.

Long-time user recalls Grafana moving fast and practically: from InfluxDB/ES-backed config to SQLite and MySQL/Postgres, then adding alerting and multiple data sources. Their team even uses Grafana with SQL as a cheap Periscope/Mode replacement.
Got through signup, shipped k8s logs to hosted Loki, and set up the data source, but could not find a way to actually explore the logs in the hosted Grafana instance.

Questions the need for Grafana: they monitor 1,000+ endpoints with shell scripts, rsync/ssh and matplotlib graphs. They say a Grafana stack carries steep spec, setup-time and complexity costs, and ask what value it adds beyond visuals.

Built live monitoring for a fleet of prototype test robots with InfluxDB and Grafana; it worked great and new data streams were simple to add. Grafana let them switch from Graphite to InfluxDB easily since it supports both.
Having rolled their own Grafana and Prometheus many times, this user says a startup that can afford Datadog should use Datadog instead.
Has monitored ~120 machines with Influx+Telegraf+Grafana for 3-4 years and is really happy with it. Their previous collectd+graphite setup consumed a significant share of infrastructure resources.
Found the software in this stack (Grafana/InfluxDB/collectd) very bloated and difficult to maintain, and prone to failing when something goes wrong. Uses Prometheus + Alertmanager instead.
